title: The seven oft-repeated
hookLine: We gave you seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an, taken as the Fatiha (15:87)

cards: A companion named Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla was praying in the mosque in Medina when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called his name. He didn't answer until he'd finished.

The Prophet reminded him, gently, that the Qur'an tells believers to answer God and His messenger when they're called. Then he said: before you leave this mosque, I'll teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an.
He took his hand. They walked toward the door. And Abu Sa'id, worried the moment would pass, said: you told me you'd teach me.
What the Prophet said at the door is in Bukhari.

teach.b: The Prophet said: alhamdu lillahi rabbil 'alamin. It is the seven oft-repeated, and the great Qur'an that I was given.
He was pointing to al-Hijr, verse eighty-seven, which Pickthall translates: "We have given thee seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the great Qur'an."

At the start of this year, you looked at the Fatiha whole, and at what happens to words said in every prayer. Today, look at what the verse calls it: a gift. And look at the very next verse, where al-Hijr takes it.

teach.h: DON'T STRAIN YOUR EYES TOWARD THEIRS.
teach.b: Verse eighty-eight, in paraphrase: so don't strain your eyes toward what We've given some of them to enjoy, and don't grieve over them, and lower your wing in tenderness for the believers.
Commentators read the two verses together. You've been handed seven verses and the great Qur'an. Don't stare longingly at other people's wealth; you're not the poor one in the room.
Al-Hijr is counted among the Meccan surahs, from years when the believers had little power and the powerful had plenty. The verse tells them what they're holding.

teach.h: TWO LIGHTS, GIVEN TO NO ONE BEFORE.
teach.b: Another hadith, in Muslim's collection, has an angel telling the Prophet: rejoice in two lights given to you that were given to no prophet before you, the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqarah.
So the Fatiha is mathani, folded and repeated, and also a treasure in the hand of someone who may have very little else. Every time it's said, the gift is opened again.

how: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in every unit of every prayer, and also at weddings, over the sick and in memory of the dead; teachers cite 15:87–88 to remind students that the Fatiha is a treasure that makes envy of others' wealth unnecessary.

games.q: you're praying when the Prophet calls your name. what does Abu Sa'id do?
games.why: he finished first. the Prophet reminded him to answer when called, then taught him the greatest surah on the way to the door.

practice: If you know the Fatiha, say it in your head one verse per breath, in Arabic or English, as if opening something given to you; if not, hold its first words: praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.
If your mind drifts to something someone else has that you don't, notice it, and come back to the words.

wordCard.voice: As-sab' al-mathani. The Fatiha's seven verses, folded and repeated in every prayer, called a gift in Surah al-Hijr.

orig.note: Arabic: "seven of the oft-repeated" (15:87), from th-n-y, to fold or repeat.

carryVoice: Your line: seven, repeated. You're not the poor one in the room. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: We have given thee seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the great Qur'an.
